{{Short description|Algebraic topology}}
In mathematics, an '''exact couple''', due to {{harvs|txt|last=Massey|first=William S.|author-link=William S. Massey|year=1952}}, is a general source of [[spectral sequence]]s. It is common especially in [[algebraic topology]]; for example, [[Serre spectral sequence]] can be constructed by first constructing an exact couple.

For the definition of an exact couple and the construction of a spectral sequence from it (which is immediate), see {{section link|Spectral_sequence#Spectral_sequence_of_an_exact_couple}}. For a basic example, see [[Bockstein spectral sequence]]. The present article covers additional materials.

==Exact couple of a filtered complex==
Let ''R'' be a [[Ring (mathematics)|ring]], which is fixed throughout the discussion. Note if ''R'' is <math>\Z</math>, then modules over ''R'' are the same thing as [[abelian group]]s.

Each filtered [[chain complex]] of modules determines an exact couple, which in turn determines a spectral sequence, as follows. Let ''C'' be a chain complex graded by [[integer]]s and suppose it is given an increasing filtration: for each integer ''p'', there is an inclusion of complexes:
:<math>F_{p-1} C \subset F_p C.</math>
From the filtration one can form the [[associated graded module|associated graded complex]]:
:<math>\operatorname{gr} C = \bigoplus_{-\infty}^\infty F_p C/F_{p-1} C,</math>
which is doubly-graded and which is the zero-th page of the spectral sequence:
:<math>E^0_{p, q} = (\operatorname{gr} C)_{p, q} = (F_p C / F_{p-1} C)_{p+q}.</math>

To get the first page, for each fixed ''p'', we look at the short [[exact sequence]] of complexes:
:<math>0 \to F_{p-1} C \to F_p C \to (\operatorname{gr}C)_p \to 0</math>
from which we obtain a long exact sequence of homologies: (''p'' is still fixed)
:<math>\cdots \to H_n(F_{p-1} C) \overset{i}\to H_n(F_p C) \overset{j} \to H_n(\operatorname{gr}(C)_p) \overset{k}\to H_{n-1}(F_{p-1} C) \to \cdots</math>
With the notation <math>D_{p, q} = H_{p+q} (F_p C), \, E^1_{p, q} = H_{p + q} (\operatorname{gr}(C)_p)</math>, the above reads:
:<math>\cdots \to D_{p - 1, q + 1} \overset{i}\to D_{p, q} \overset{j} \to E^1_{p, q} \overset{k}\to D_{p - 1, q} \to \cdots,</math>
which is precisely an exact couple and <math>E^1</math> is a complex with the differential <math>d = j \circ k</math>. The derived couple of this exact couple gives the second page and we iterate. In the end, one obtains the complexes <math>E^r_{*, *}</math> with the differential ''d'':
:<math>E^r_{p, q} \overset{k}\to D^r_{p - 1, q} \overset{{}^r j}\to E^r_{p - r, q + r - 1}.</math>

The next lemma gives a more explicit formula for the spectral sequence; in particular, it shows the spectral sequence constructed above is the same one in more traditional direct construction,<ref>{{harvnb|Weibel|1994|loc=The Construction 5.4.6.}}</ref> in which one uses the formula below as definition (cf. [[Spectral sequence#The spectral sequence of a filtered complex]]).

{{math_theorem|Lemma|Let <math>A^r_p = \{ c \in F_p C \mid d(c) \in F_{p-r} C \}</math>, which inherits <math>\mathbb{Z}</math>-grading from <math>F_pC </math>. Then for each ''p''
:<math>E^r_{p, *} \simeq {A^r_p \over d(A^{r-1}_{p+r-1}) + A^{r-1}_{p-1}}.</math>}}
Sketch of proof:<ref>{{harvnb|May|loc=Proof of (7.3)}}</ref><ref>{{harvnb|Weibel|1994|loc=Theorem 5.9.4.}}</ref> Remembering <math>d = j \circ k</math>, it is easy to see:
:<math>Z^r= k^{-1} (\operatorname{im} i^r), \, B^r = j (\operatorname{ker} i^r),</math>
where they are viewed as subcomplexes of <math>E^1</math>.

We will write the bar for <math>F_p C \to F_p C / F_{p-1} C</math>. Now, if <math>[\overline{x}] \in Z^{r-1}_{p, q} \subset E^1_{p, q}</math>, then <math>k([\overline{x}]) = i^{r-1}([y])</math> for some <math>[y] \in D_{p - r, q + r - 1} = H_{p+q-1}(F_p C)</math>. On the other hand, remembering ''k'' is a connecting homomorphism, <math>k([\overline{x}]) = [d(x)]</math> where ''x'' is a representative living in <math>(F_p C)_{p + q}</math>. Thus, we can write: <math>d(x) - i^{r-1}(y) = d(x')</math> for some <math>x' \in F_{p-1}C</math>. Hence, <math>[\overline{x}] \in Z^r_p \Leftrightarrow x \in A^r_p</math> modulo <math>F_{p-1} C</math>, yielding <math>Z_p^r \simeq (A^r_p + F_{p-1}C)/F_{p-1} C</math>.

Next, we note that a class in <math>\operatorname{ker}(i^{r-1}: H_{p+q}(F_pC) \to H_{p+q}(F_{p + r - 1} C))</math> is represented by a cycle ''x'' such that <math>x \in d(F_{p+r-1} C)</math>. Hence, since ''j'' is induced by <math>\overline{\cdot}</math>, <math>B^{r-1}_p = j (\operatorname{ker} i^{r-1}) \simeq (d(A^{r-1}_{p+r-1}) + F_{p-1} C)/F_{p-1} C</math>.

We conclude: since <math>A^r_p \cap F_{p-1} C = A^{r-1}_{p-1}</math>,
:<math>E^r_{p, *} = {Z^{r-1}_p \over B^{r-1}_p} \simeq {A^r_p + F_{p-1} C \over d(A^{r-1}_{p+r-1}) + F_{p-1}C} \simeq {A^r_p \over d(A^{r-1}_{p+r-1}) + A^{r-1}_{p-1}}. \qquad \square</math>

{{math_theorem|Theorem|If <math>C = \cup_p F_p C</math> and for each ''n'' there is an integer <math>s(n)</math> such that <math>F_{s(n)} C_n = 0</math>, then the spectral sequence ''E''<sup>''r''</sup> converges to <math>H_*(C)</math>; that is, <math>E^\infty_{p, q} = F_p H_{p+q}(C)/F_{p-1} H_{p+q}(C)</math>.}}
Proof: See the last section of May. <math>\square</math>

== Exact couple of a double complex ==
A [[double complex]] determines two exact couples; whence, the two spectral sequences, are as follows. (Some authors call the two spectral sequences horizontal and vertical<!--; this is either helpful or confusing -->.) Let <math>K^{p,q}</math> be a double complex.<ref>We prefer cohomological notation here since the applications are often in algebraic geometry.</ref> With the notation <math>G^p = \bigoplus_{i \ge p} K^{i, *}</math>, for each with fixed ''p'', we have the exact sequence of cochain complexes:

:<math>0 \to G^{p+1} \to G^p \to K^{p, *} \to 0.</math>

Taking cohomology of it gives rise to an exact couple:

:<math>\cdots \to D^{p, q} \overset{j}\to E_1^{p, q} \overset{k}\to \cdots</math>

<!--where we used the notation-->
By symmetry, that is, by switching first and second indexes, one also obtains the other exact couple.

==Example: Serre spectral sequence==
{{expand section|date=November 2025|reason=Needs a concrete, worked example (e.g., the Hopf fibration $S^1 \to S^3 \to S^2$) to illustrate the page computations and convergence.}}
The [[Serre spectral sequence]] is a powerful tool used to compute the homology or cohomology of the total space of a [[fibration]]. It expresses the [[singular homology]] of the total space ''E'' in terms of the homology of the base space ''B'' and the fiber ''F''.

The sequence arises from a fibration:
:<math>F \to E \xrightarrow{p} B.</math>

For the sake of transparency, we often initially consider the simplified case when the spaces are [[CW complex]]es, the fiber ''F'' is [[Connected space|connected]], and the base ''B'' is [[Simply connected space|simply connected]]. In this scenario, the action of the [[fundamental group]] of the base on the [[Homology (mathematics)|homology]] of the fiber is trivial, allowing for the use of constant coefficients. The second page of the homology spectral sequence is given by a [[Künneth theorem|Künneth]]-like tensor product structure:
:<math>E^2_{p,q} \cong H_p(B; \mathbb{Z}) \otimes H_q(F; \mathbb{Z}) \implies H_{p+q}(E; \mathbb{Z})</math>

The general case involves more technicality (namely, [[local coefficient system|local coefficient systems]]) to handle the non-trivial action of <math>\pi_1(B)</math> on <math>H_*(F)</math>. The <math>E^2</math> page then becomes a group [[homology (mathematics)|homology]] or [[group cohomology|cohomology]] group:
:<math>E^2_{p,q} \cong H_p(B; H_q(F)).</math>
